subject: business-studies
title: External Stretch Adventure
welcome_lead: Exam-style stretch. Evaluate competition, recession responses and global influences.
meta_desc: GCSE Business Studies stretch — evaluating competition, recession, and global pressures on UK firms.
final_note: You can evaluate competitive pressures, recession responses and global influences on firms.

concepts.def: Rival firms targeting the same customers
Two quarters of negative economic growth
World trade and culture becoming more linked
Tax on imports raising their price
Government payment to lower business costs
Group lobbying firms to change behaviour

walkthroughs.body_html:
More rivals = downward pressure on prices and margins.

Firms respond by differentiating (USP), improving quality, lowering costs, or finding niches.
Demand falls in a recession. Firms cut costs (delay hiring, reduce stock), focus on cash flow, and target value-conscious customers.

Globalisation offers bigger markets but also tougher competition and currency risk.

Tariffs and subsidies can swing the playing field overnight.

mcqs.q: What are the four Ps of the marketing mix?
options: The four Ps are Product, Price, Profit, and People.
Product, Price, Place (distribution), and Promotion — the controllable variables a business uses to satisfy customers and achieve objectives.
Share prices are set by the government each morning.
The four Ps are Planning, Producing, Promoting, and Profit.

mcqs.q: Why are cash flow and profit different on different time-scales?
options: Profit is recognised when a sale is made (even on credit); cash flow is when money actually moves. A profitable sale today may produce no cash for 60 days while bills are due — creating a cash-flow problem despite profit.
Cash flow and profit are the same thing measured differently.
The four Ps are Planning, Producing, Promoting, and Profit.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.

mcqs.q: Why does a company's share price change?
options: Share prices go up when a company makes more money this year.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Share prices reflect investors' expectations about future profits — driven by company performance, sector trends, economic conditions, and market sentiment.
Share prices are set by the government each morning.
